query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered promising for high-heat wear-resistant use and is suitable for thin-film applications; because bulk preparation is expensive, applying it as a coating on a conventional metal is more practical. Earlier studies reported improved wear or mechanical performance from high-entropy-alloy coatings on Al, Ni, and titanium-alloy substrates, and simulations of FeNiCrCoCu on Cu indicated that sliding speed affects tangential and normal forces. Other work associated composition and grain size with changes in wear damage. However, most prior studies examined a limited operating regime or the properties of the alloys themselves rather than the overall wear resistance of coatings under varied thermal conditions. Subject to retaining FeNiCrCoCu as a coating on a Cu matrix, what single intervention could improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its causal mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to an unchanged coating in matched tests, the boundaries within which it should hold, supporting evidence from the introduction, and an experiment with a clear rejection criterion for both the predicted outcome and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a nanoscale grain-refinement treatment to the FeNiCrCoCu coating prior to deposition will enhance its overall wear resistance across varied thermal and contact regimes by stabilizing a high-density of grain boundaries that suppress thermally activated dislocation motion and mitigate abrasive wear.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix with conventional grain size and no specific grain-boundary engineering.
generation.intervention: Apply a cryogenic milling or severe plastic deformation pre-treatment to the FeNiCrCoCu powder to achieve nanoscale grain refinement before coating deposition.
generation.conditions: Sliding contact across varied thermal regimes (elevated temperatures) and varied contact pressures, simulating high-heat wear-resistant use.
generation.structural_mediator: High-density grain boundaries acting as barriers to dislocation glide and sites for dynamic strain aging, preventing thermal softening.
generation.mechanism: The refined grain structure increases the Hall-Petch strengthening effect and provides a higher density of grain boundaries that impede dislocation motion even at elevated temperatures, thereby reducing the rate of wear damage compared to coarse-grained counterparts.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nanoscale-grained FeNiCrCoCu coating will exhibit a significantly lower specific wear rate and reduced tangential force fluctuations compared to the conventional-grained coating under identical sliding conditions across the tested thermal range.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating on Cu matrix with conventional grain size, prepared without nanoscale refinement.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for sliding speeds and temperatures where thermally activated dislocation motion is the dominant wear mechanism; it may not hold if the temperature exceeds the recrystallization threshold of the nanoscale grains, causing grain growth and loss of strengthening.
generation.uncertainty: The provided evidence records are empty, so the specific quantitative relationship between grain size and wear resistance for this specific alloy system under varied thermal conditions is not established in the supplied text. The hypothesis relies on general materials science principles (Hall-Petch) rather than specific cited data for this system.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on Cu substrates: Set A (Control) with conventional grain size and Set B (Intervention) with nanoscale grain refinement. Subject both to a sliding wear test across a gradient of temperatures (e.g., 25°C to 400°C) and varying contact pressures.
measurements: Specific wear rate (volume loss per unit distance)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if Set B shows a specific wear rate equal to or greater than Set A at any temperature below the recrystallization threshold, or if post-test analysis reveals that the nanoscale grains in Set B have coarsened to a size comparable to Set A without a corresponding increase in wear resistance.
